clinician.final_diagnosis: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) with multisystem involvement (cutaneous, CNS, and bone)
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old white male presented with a 6-year history of progressive neurological symptoms (imbalance, diplopia, slurred speech, progressing to inability to walk, dysphagia, and dysarthria) and a concurrent 2-year history of a partially ulcerated, circular, erythematous infiltrate plaque (2 cm) on the right scapular region. Skin biopsy revealed histiocytic cell proliferation with atypical features and eosinophilic infiltration of the reticular dermis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD1a, protein S100, and Langerin, confirming the diagnosis of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis. Brain MRI on admission demonstrated diffuse encephalic volumetric reduction and multiple hyperintense lesions on T2 and FLAIR sequences, predominantly affecting the cerebellar bridge and peduncles, consistent with CNS-LCH involvement explaining the cerebellar and brainstem signs. The patient received methylprednisolone pulse therapy without response and subsequently developed diabetes insipidus, indicating hypothalamic-pituitary involvement. Follow-up MRI two months later revealed an expansive right parietal bone lesion with extra-axial calcification, meningeal involvement, and encephalic compression, confirming multisystem LCH with bone involvement.
